title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Ap4A Production by LysRS During HIV Infection
content: The incorporation of the correct amino acid during translation is essential for life, and incorporation of the wrong amino acid can produce toxic proteins, triggering cell death. The fidelity of translation is ensured by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (aaRS), a family of proteins that covalently attach specific amino acids to their corresponding tRNAs. Lysyl-tRNA synthetase (LysRS), for instance, aminoacylates all tRNAs coding for lysine in cells (tRNALys), making it essential to life. Beyond the essential role of LysRS in translation fidelity, LysRS moonlights as the main producer of diadenosine tetraphosphate (Ap4A), a signaling molecule with diverse biological roles in immunity and gene regulation. LysRS is also hijacked by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), making it a pro-viral factor required for infectivity. Despite the importance of LysRS in human health and diseases, and its involvement in seemingly disparate pathways, it remains poorly understood how this enzyme switches between its diverse functions. For my thesis, I aim to define mechanistically how LysRS not only ensures translation fidelity but also how LysRS is co-opted by HIV to reveal new interfaces that can be targeted by next-generation antiviral strategies. Using electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA) we showed that LysRS binds DNA-RNA hybrids with similar affinity as tRNA. This binding is dependent on the length of the DNA-RNA hybrid with longer length promoting tighter affinity. To visualize this ribonucleoprotein complex, we are using single particle CryoEM. Preliminary data suggest that the complex denatures at the air-water interface contrasting with the complex formed with tRNA for which we solved its cryoEM structure at a global resolution of 2.82 Å at NCCAT. This structure reveals an asymmetric complex prone for catalysis while the organization of the homodimeric LysRS is similar to the one seen in previous crystal structures. Overall, this work paves the way to defining how LysRS’s function is regulated by nucleic acids binding to control gene expression and the immune response.
